title: 2 Peter
subtitle: a farewell letter: grow, remember, and wait for the day
lead: 2 Peter is a short letter, three chapters and 61 verses, written as the last words of the apostle Peter. He knows his death is near (1:14), and he writes so that the church will remember the apostles' teaching after he is gone.

It has three movements. First, growth: God has given believers everything for life and godliness, so they should add goodness, knowledge, self-control and love to their faith. Second, warning: false teachers have come, much as Jude describes, and God knows how to judge them and rescue his people. Third, hope: mockers ask where Jesus' promised coming is, and Peter answers that God is patient, the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and a new heavens and new earth are coming. No book of the New Testament has been more doubted, and none says more strongly that believers share in God's own nature (1:4).
facts: Traditionally the apostle Peter ("Simeon Peter," 1:1). Most critical scholars: a follower writing in Peter's name after his death. See "Who wrote it?" below.
If Peter wrote it, shortly before his death in Rome in the mid 60s AD. If a follower wrote it, most often placed late in the first century (Richard Bauckham: AD 80–90) or early in the second.
"Those who were given a faith just as precious as ours" (1:1); if 3:1 refers to 1 Peter, the churches of Asia Minor (1 Peter 1:1).
A letter in the form of a farewell testament, with an extended warning (chapter 2) reworked from Jude
Greek, an elaborate, high style with many rare words, very different from 1 Peter
Papyrus 72 (third or fourth century), which contains all of 1 and 2 Peter and Jude
authorship: It opens "From Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ" (1:1), speaks of Jesus' word about Peter's death (1:14), claims that the writer heard the voice on the holy mountain (1:16–18), calls itself "the second letter" (3:1), and calls Paul "our beloved brother" (3:15).

Most critical scholars hold that 2 Peter was written in Peter's name after his death. J. N. D. Kelly wrote (as Michael Kruger quotes him) that "scarcely anyone nowadays doubts that 2 Peter is pseudonymous," and Bart Ehrman calls it the New Testament book most widely judged pseudonymous. Their arguments: (1) Dependence on Jude: most of chapter 2 reworks Jude, which most think came first, and an apostle would hardly need to borrow from a lesser figure. (2) Style: the Greek is ornate and very different from 1 Peter's; Jerome already reported that many denied the letter to Peter "on account of its difference from the first in style." (3) A later setting: "the fathers" have died (3:4), the readers have "your apostles" (3:2), and Paul's letters are a known collection set beside "the other Scriptures" (3:16). (4) The testament form, a well-known way of writing in a great figure's name. (5) Thin early attestation: Origen in the 200s said a second letter was "doubtful," and Eusebius (about 325) said it was not received as canonical, though many found it useful. Richard Bauckham argued that the first readers would have recognized the testament form, so that "the pseudepigraphal device is therefore not a fraudulent means of claiming apostolic authority" (in his Word Biblical Commentary, as quoted by Ray Van Neste); Ehrman, by contrast, calls such writings forgeries.

A minority of scholars defend the letter's claim. Michael Green, in a 1960 lecture, argued that the different style could come from Peter's use of different secretaries for the two letters, as Jerome had already suggested (Letter 120: Peter used "different interpreters"), and concluded: "It cannot be shown conclusively that Peter was the author; but it has yet to be shown convincingly that he was not." Michael Kruger (1999) reviewed the arguments and found the case for pseudonymity "too incomplete and insufficient to warrant the dogmatic conclusions," concluding that "we have no reason to doubt the epistle's own claims." Defenders add: the personal memory of the mountain and the voice, in words that match no Gospel exactly; the old Hebrew name Simeon; the possibility that "the fathers" are Israel's ancestors; Paul's letters circulating in his own lifetime (Colossians 4:16); and the early church's rejection of writings it knew to be forged.

Some think a disciple wrote at Peter's direction or soon after his death, faithfully passing on his teaching. Calvin, who received the letter as Scripture, wrote, "I do not here recognize the language of Peter," and suggested "that some one of his disciples set forth in writing, by his command" what Peter wanted said. Peter Davids leaves the question open: "we by the nature of the case cannot know from historical investigation whether this is in some sense actual or is a pseudepigraphical attribution" (as Ernst Baasland's review of Davids quotes him).

Among critical scholars, pseudonymity is clearly the majority view. The traditional view, that Peter is the author, is held by the churches' historic teaching and by a minority of scholars today, mostly evangelical and some Catholic and Orthodox. The Plain follows the text as written: "Simeon Peter."

audience.to: Believers who "were given a faith just as precious as ours" (1:1). The letter names no city. If "the second letter" (3:1) means 1 Peter, these are the churches of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia in what is now Turkey (1 Peter 1:1), mostly Gentile converts living as a small minority in Greek cities. They had received the gospel from apostles (3:2), knew Paul's letters (3:15–16), and spoke the language of Greek moral philosophy that the letter uses (1:3–7). Teachers inside their churches were mocking the promise of Christ's coming, living loosely, and offering "freedom" to new converts.
audience.why: To be the apostle's lasting reminder (1:12–15; 3:1–2), so that the churches would not be carried away when the apostles were gone. The letter calls the readers to grow in the qualities that make their calling firm (1:5–11), grounds their hope in the apostles' eyewitness testimony and the prophets (1:16–21), exposes the false teachers (chapter 2), and answers the mockers' claim that Christ will not come and God does not judge (chapter 3). Knowing the readers explains the method: to Greek-speaking converts tempted by a philosophy of no judgment, the letter speaks their moral language but insists that God has acted in history (the flood) and will act again.
views: The most common view: 3:1 refers to 1 Peter, and the readers are the churches of Asia Minor.
Others note that 1 Peter says little about false teachers or the delay of the coming, and think 3:1 refers to a lost letter, or that the address is general, to the whole church.

Epicureans taught that the gods do not judge. David deSilva says that the majority of scholars now place the rival teachers against this background; Peter Davids follows Jerome Neyrey in placing the readers among Gentiles influenced by Epicurean teaching (as Ernst Baasland's review of Davids reports). Others think the problem was simply the long wait and the death of the first generation.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads 2 Peter as a letter to Greek-speaking churches, most likely in Asia Minor, facing teachers who mocked the promise of Christ's coming and offered "freedom." Asks what the farewell form, the Greek moral vocabulary and the Genesis examples meant to its first readers.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the letter and when, how it used Jude, what "the fathers," "your apostles" and "all his letters" imply, why the early church doubted it, and how the text came down to us (Papyrus 72, the hard reading of 3:10).

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the farewell-testament form, the chain of virtues (1:5–7), the elaborate Greek style, the long sentence of 2:4–9, and the repeated words: knowledge, remind, promise, found.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's use of Israel's Scriptures and Jewish tradition: the Watchers in Tartarus, Noah the preacher, righteous Lot, Balaam son of Bosor, Psalm 90:4, the day of the Lord and the new heavens and new earth, and the Jewish farewell testament.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads 2 Peter as the churches have: its slow acceptance into the canon, 1:4 and the Orthodox doctrine of theosis, 1:20–21 on inspiration and who interprets Scripture, 2:1 and 2:20–22 in the debates over the atonement and falling away, and 3:16 on Paul's letters as Scripture.

sections.b: Read it as a last will. The writer is about to "lay aside" his tent (1:14) and wants three things remembered: grow in Christ (chapter 1), recognize false teachers (chapter 2), and keep waiting for the Lord's coming (chapter 3). Listen for the repeated words: "knowledge" of Christ, "remind," "promise," "eager," and "found." Read chapter 2 beside Jude 4–16 to see how the writer used his source.

Most of Jude 4–18 appears again, reworked, in 2 Peter 2:1–3:3. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude; a minority, including Luther, thought the reverse (Luther wrote that Jude took "nearly all its words" from 2 Peter). In this site's Plain, the two are translated the same way where the Greek matches and differently where it differs. See the topic page .

The two letters claim the same writer, but their Greek is very different: 1 Peter is clear and steady; 2 Peter is ornate, with many rare words. The difference was noticed early. Jerome reported that many denied 2 Peter to Peter because of its style, and elsewhere explained the difference by Peter's use of different interpreters (Letter 120). The letters share some themes (the flood and Noah's eight, 1 Peter 3:20; 2:5; the prophets, 1 Peter 1:10–12; 1:19–21; holy living while waiting for the end) but differ in others: 1 Peter is about suffering under pressure from outside, 2 Peter about false teaching inside.

sections.h: 2 Peter among the books of the Bible
sections.b: No New Testament book had a harder road into the canon. Papyrus 72, from the third or fourth century, is the earliest copy. In the 200s Origen wrote that Peter "has left one acknowledged epistle; perhaps also a second, but this is doubtful." Eusebius (about 325) said that the second letter "does not belong to the canon," though because many found it useful it was studied with the other Scriptures, and he listed it among the disputed books "recognized by many." Jerome (392) says many rejected it because of its style. Yet Athanasius's list of AD 367 includes "of Peter, two," and from then on it was received everywhere. Calvin doubted that Peter himself wrote it but would not reject it: "to repudiate it is what I dread." Every major church today counts it as Scripture.

Like Jude, 2 Peter draws on Jewish ways of reading Scripture, but more cautiously: it names no book outside the Bible. Its examples still carry Jewish tradition: angels thrown into Tartarus, a Greek name for the underworld that 1 Enoch also uses (1 Enoch 20:2); Noah as a "herald of righteousness," as Josephus and the Sibylline Oracles describe him; "righteous" Lot, as in the Wisdom of Solomon; and Psalm 90:4 used to measure God's time, as in Jubilees. Its hope, "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17), is the prophets' hope.

sections.h: The Greek text behind the Plain
sections.b: For the Catholic Letters, NA28 adopted the text of the Editio Critica Maior, and where the editions divide, the Plain usually follows NA28 (for example 2:6, 2:18, 3:11, 3:16 and 3:18). It departs from NA28 in two places, both explained in the manuscript notes. At 3:6 it keeps the plural "Through these" with every other edition. At 3:10 it keeps "will be found," the reading of the oldest Greek manuscripts, rather than NA28's conjecture "will not be found," which no Greek manuscript has; in English the Plain renders it "will lie exposed."

spec.title: Claude's theory: a letter about memory
spec.body: This is my own reading. 2 Peter is built around remembering and forgetting. The person without the virtues "has forgotten" the cleansing of his sins (1:9); Peter wants to "keep reminding" them (1:12–13) and leave them a way to "recall" his teaching after his death (1:15); this second letter rouses them "by reminding" (3:1); the mockers' error is something they "want" to let "escape" them (3:5), while the readers must not let God's time-scale "escape" them (3:8). I suggest that the letter treats forgetting, not ignorance, as the root danger: the false teachers know the way of righteousness and turn back (2:21). Commentators note the reminder theme; reading forgetfulness as the letter's diagnosis of the false teachers is my own emphasis.

prompts: The voice on the holy mountain (1:16–18)

Three fishermen in simple tunics shielding their eyes on a rocky mountaintop as a bright cloud spreads over them; in the center a figure in clothes shining white like light; rays and the faint shape of sound waves coming down from the cloud; below, the hills of Galilee and a lake in the distance. Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

reading: The standard technical commentary; argues that 2 Peter is a testament written in Peter's name, probably AD 80–90.
Michael Green, 2 Peter and Jude (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries, rev. ed. 1987)
A readable defense of Peter as the author.
Peter H. Davids, The Letters of 2 Peter and Jude (Pillar, 2006)
Clear and fair; leaves the authorship question open.
Gene L. Green, Jude and 2 Peter (Baker Exegetical Commentary, 2008)
A detailed commentary on the Greek, strong on the Greek and Roman setting.
Jerome H. Neyrey, 2 Peter, Jude (Anchor Bible, 1993)
Reads the opponents against Epicurean philosophy and the social world of honor and shame.
Michael J. Kruger, "The Authenticity of 2 Peter," Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 42 (1999)
A full review of the arguments, defending the letter's claim.
Al Wolters, "Worldview and Textual Criticism in 2 Peter 3:10," Westminster Theological Journal 49 (1987)
The case for reading 3:10 as refining, not annihilation.
